sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Ligurian Fault System (Larroque et al., 2011) is a NE-SW striking, S-verging, about 80-km-long reverse system located in the northern Ligurian Sea, a few kilometers south of the Italy-France boundary region.
The northern Ligurian margin is characterized by a narrow continental shelf (from 200 m-to 2 km-wide between Nice and Imperia), and a 20 km-wide, steep continental slope (with an average slope of 8 degrees, and a maximum slope of 20 degrees) down to 2600 m depth. The continental slope is affected by numerous scarps due to sediment failures and sub-marine landslides (e.g. Migeon et al., 2011).
Based on the interpretation of high-resolution multibeam bathymetric data collected during the MALISAR surveys (2006, 2007, and 2008), Larroque et al. (2009, 2011, 2012) identified a large number of submarine failures along the northern margin of the Ligurian basin. The observed morphological features attest to recent and significant deformation. These data allowed the identification of the Ligurian Fault System, a transpressive system of Plio-Quaternary faults, consistent with the present-day kinematics (Larroque et al., 2009, 2011, 2012).
Near the southwestern border of the Ligurian Fault System, Larroque et al. (2011) reported evidence of Quaternary activity along the "Marcel Fault", a N60Â°E, 10-km-long scarp at the foot of the continental slope.
According to the same investigators, near the northeastern border of the Ligurian Fault System, off the Imperia coastline, the southeastern flank of a large elongated promontory is bounded by a network of N60Â°E faults. This 40-km-long ridge lies above the continental slope and is referred to as Imperia Promontory. The southeastward facing flank of the ridge corresponds to the steeper part of the eastern margin of the Ligurian Fault System, where the mean and the maximum slope angle reach 12Â° and 22Â°, respectively. At the top of the promontory, the Messinian erosion surface and at least two unconformities are tilted northwestward. Larroque et al. (2011) proposed a long term uplift rate of 0.40-0.53 mm/y for this structure during the Plio-Quaternary.
North of the Imperia Promontory, the high-resolution bathymetry shows a peculiar submarine drainage network. A number of canyons lying between Imperia and Savona initially flow southeastward, i.e. perpendicular to the coast, but are then deflected northeasterward consistent with recent uplift of the Promontory.
A paleo-canyon seen at the top of the Promontory could be the ancient outlet of one of these canyons, abandoned during the uplift of the ridge, as if it were a terrestrial wind gap. This peculiar drainage pattern is controlled by the growth of the anticline of the Imperia Promontory, which produces tilting of the erosion surface described above. Larroque et al. (2011) proposed that the uplift is generated by the large reverse fault that bounds the promontory to the southeast.
We associated the growing anticline of the Imperia Promontory with the source of the 23 February 1887 earthquake. This event caused significant damage and numerous casualties in northwestern Italy and southeastern France. The event was followed by a tsunami observed along a 250 km section of the coast, from Genoa to Cannes, with a maximum run-up of 2 m near Imperia. It is difficult to assess with precision the epicentral location and the magnitude for such a historical and offshore event, therefore the identification of the seismogenic source has been the subject of a long debate. We believe that a specific segment of the Ligurian Fault System, identified by new morphotectonic data acquired by recent marine geophysical surveys, is responsible for the 23 February 1887 earthquake.
We propose the following geometrical parameters for the source: the strike is chosen according to that of the Imperia Promontory; the rake is assumed to be pure reverse faulting, based on geodynamic considerations and on the stress field retrieved from focal mechanisms; the length and the down-dip width are constrained by scaling relationships with the magnitude of the 1887 earthquake and by the location of the Saorge-Taggia transverse lineament. We infer a long-term uplift rate for the Plio-Quaternary from three assumptions: 1) prior to the uplift of the Imperia Promontory, the continental slope had a constant inclination; 2) the uplift started around 3-4 Ma; and 3) the Imperia Promontory raised as much as 600 m above the continental slope.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the causative fault of the 1887 earthquake purely reverse?
2) Does the fault terminate against the Saorge-Taggia transverse lineament that cuts the western Ligurian coast?
3) Are similar events likely to occur all along the 80-km-long transpressive Ligurian Fault System?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Fanucci et al. (1989)
These workers used selected focal mechanisms to point out the purely compressional nature of earthquake-related deformation in the western Ligurian Sea (offshore between Albenga and Nice). This evidence is found in contrast with available neotectonic evidence, which according to these investigators does not suggest the existence of significant compression. Based on a limited number of focal solutions, Fanucci et al. (1989) also discuss evidence for transtensional deformation along the Ligurian margin (that is, inland).
Ferrari (1991)
This is a comprehensive summary of all the investigations of the 1887 earthquake by contemporary workers and a revised list of over 1000 intensity reports. This investigator located the epicenter about 20 km offshore south of Oneglia and revises the magnitude up to 6.4-6.5 from the 5.6 estimate originally proposed by Capponi et al. (1985).
Bethoux et al. (1992)
These investigators analyzed the focal mechanism of several shocks in the magnitude range 3.0 to 6.3 that occurred in the western Ligurian Sea starting with 1963. They conclude that all the events indicate compressional tectonics, but also that the stress regime is more diverse than previously thought and that the P-axes exhibit rotations from nearly N-S to nearly E-W. The compressional regime is interpreted as due to lateral expulsion of the southwestern Alps along the Apulian indenter.
Augliera et al. (1994)
These investigators discussed the general seismotectonic framework of the Western Ligurian Sea combining information from background seismicity and evidence from reflection seismology profiles. These investigators stress the different nature of the onshore area, which is characterized by N120Â°-trending reactivated faults, and the margin-offshore area, which is dominated by roughly N160Â°-trending younger faults. These offshore structures correspond to transverse faults perpendicular to the margin and were created during rifting of the Ligurian Sea. A series of sedimentary basins aligned ENE-SSW (i.e., parallel to the margin) and located 30-40 km from the present coast are bound by a major
ENE-trending normal fault, but no evidence of its activity exists in the seismological record. In contrast, seismicity suggests compression along a roughly N-S trend, which is suggestive of the transpressional nature of the margin. According to Augliera et al. (1994), seismicity concentrates along zones of weakness or reactivated structures, and therefore does not appear to have a "primary" nature with respect to the present stress field. No specific interpretation is given concerning the source of the 1887 earthquake, which is located halfway between the coast and the system of offshore normal faults.
Eva and Rabinovich (1997)
This paper proposed a numerical model of the tsunami associated with the 1887 earthquake. Their best fitting model involves normal faulting along an ENE-trending fault (south side up) located 20 to 30 km offshore in front of Imperia. This result is interpreted as being consistent with the postulated existence of a system of large normal faults located just at the foot of the continental margin and parallel to the coast. This system would be segmented by inferred transform faults perpendicular to it and to the coast.
Courboulex et al. (1998)
This paper discussed the source parameters of the 21 April 1995, Ventimiglia earthquake (Ml 4.7). According to these investigators, this well-recorded event occurred just beneath the coastline at a depth of about 9 km and had a dominantly reverse mechanism with a strong strike-slip component. Courboulex et al. discuss various lines of evidence suggesting that the event was generated by a compressional regime and occurred along one of a series of old NW-SE transverse faults that cut the Alpine margin in several narrow slices.
Larroque et al. (2011)
These investigators presented new high-resolution bathymetric data (EM300 multibeam bathymetry, 25 m gridding) collected during the MALISAR surveys (2006, 2007 and 2008). They focus on two areas of the northern Ligurian margin where they reveal recent and active deformation. They describe a set of N60Â°E scarps, previously unknown, that cut across the continental slope. According to these investigators, these scarps are right above fault zones. They identified the 10-km-long Marcel Fault and the 40-km-long Imperia Promontory. They propose a long term uplift rate of 0.40-0.53 mm/year for the Imperia Promontory during the Plio-Quaternary.
Larroque et al. (2012)
These investigators presented their better assessment of the seismic source responsible for the 1887 Ligurian earthquake from macroseismicity, active tectonic and tsunami modelling. Their proposal for the 1887 event is the activation of a 35-km-long, 17-km-wide and N55Â°E striking fault, dipping 16Â° to the north, with a coseismic slip of 1.5 m, and a focal depth of 15 km.
